goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35 stores feed HTML with `cook_method: raw_html`, bypassing sanitization and enabling stored XSS when `post.cooked` is rendered

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35, the code does `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` and then passes it to `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`. In TopicEmbed.import (app/models/topic_embed.rb), the content is passed to PostCreator with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. When cook_method is raw_html, the Post.cook method (app/models/post.rb lines 131-133) returns `raw` directly without any sanitization: `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. This raw HTML is then stored and rendered via `raw post.cooked` in the view (app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 17). The RSS feed content could contain malicious JavaScript, and since it bypasses both cooking/sanitization and is rendered with Rails' `raw` helper, this creates a stored XSS vulnerability. The finding correctly identifies that feed HTML is stored with raw_html cook method and rendered unsanitized.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 uses `open(url)` with redirects while validating only the initial hostname, allowing an allowlisted host to redirect requests to internal services (SSRF)

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code uses `open(url).read` where `url` comes from user input (the embed_url parameter). The validation at line 11 only checks if the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://' using a regex. However, there's no validation that the URL's hostname matches the embeddable_host setting before making the HTTP request. The embeddable_host check happens in topic_retriever.rb for the embed_url parameter, but in import_remote, the url is passed directly to open() without hostname validation. If an attacker controls a server on the allowlisted embeddable_host, they could set up a redirect to internal services. The open-uri library follows redirects by default, so a request to an allowed host could redirect to internal services like http://169.254.169.254/ (AWS metadata) or internal network resources. This is a valid SSRF concern - the initial URL hostname is not validated against embeddable_host in import_remote, and even if it were, redirects could bypass that check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:17 performs a non-atomic lookup followed by `TopicEmbed.create!`, allowing concurrent imports to race and causing one worker to raise `RecordNotUnique` and terminate

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:17, the code does `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` followed by `TopicEmbed.create!` if embed is blank. This is indeed a classic TOCTOU (time-of-check-time-of-use) race condition. The database has a unique index on embed_url (seen in the migration at db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb: `add_index :topic_embeds, :embed_url, unique: true`), so concurrent imports of the same URL could both pass the `embed.blank?` check and then one would fail with RecordNotUnique when trying to create. This is a real concurrency bug - the code should use find_or_create_by with proper locking, or rescue the unique constraint violation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 synchronously polls and processes the entire feed on every distinct cache miss, allowing attackers or concurrent visitors to amplify expensive full-feed work despite per-URL throttling

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:41, the perform_retrieve method calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}) synchronously when feed_polling_enabled? is true. The throttling in retrieved_recently? is per-URL (using 'retrieved:#{@embed_url}' as the key), so different embed URLs will each trigger their own cache miss. When a cache miss occurs for any new URL, the entire RSS feed is polled and processed synchronously via poll_feed. This means N different embed URLs could each trigger a full feed poll within the 60-second window, as the throttle only prevents the same URL from being retrieved twice. This is a real performance/DoS concern - attackers could request many different embed URLs to amplify expensive feed polling work.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:62 incorrectly rewrites protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/image.png` as paths on the article host, breaking links and images

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 53-70, the code checks if href/src start_with?('/') and then prepends the prefix. Protocol-relative URLs like '//cdn.example.com/image.png' do start with '/', so they would be incorrectly rewritten to something like 'http://eviltrout.com/cdn.example.com/image.png'. This is a real bug - the code should check for '//' prefix first to avoid mangling protocol-relative URLs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:6 limits `embed_url` to 255 characters without matching validation, causing valid longer URLs to fail insertion and potentially leave embeds perpetually loading

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the migration in db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb, the embed_url column is defined as `t.string :embed_url, null: false`. In Rails, a string column without an explicit limit defaults to 255 characters in most databases. However, examining the TopicEmbed model in app/models/topic_embed.rb, there is only `validates_presence_of :embed_url` but no length validation. The import method in TopicEmbed.import does check `url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` but doesn't validate length. If a URL longer than 255 characters is passed, the database insertion would fail with a truncation or constraint error. This is a real potential issue - URLs can legitimately exceed 255 characters (especially with query parameters), and the code doesn't handle this case, which could cause the embed to fail silently or throw an error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:27 performs `SETNX` and `EXPIRE` separately, so a crash between them can leave a permanent throttle key that prevents the URL from ever being retrieved

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition in lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 26-28. The code uses `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` followed by `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` as separate operations. If the process crashes or is killed between these two calls, the key will be set without an expiration, causing it to persist indefinitely. This would permanently block retrieval of that specific embed_url. The correct approach would be to use a single atomic operation like `SET key value EX 60 NX` (available in Redis 2.6.12+) or use a Lua script. This is a real bug that could cause permanent throttling of specific URLs.
